paper.citation: Delgadillo BE, Montz F, Ward BJ Jr, Herson AB, Toldi JP. Current evidence for the use of jugular vein compression collars in sport: a systematic review. Curr Sports Med Rep. 2025;24(1):18-27.
paper.abstract: This systematic review followed PRISMA and included 15 studies of external jugular vein compression collars in high school football and soccer, hockey, and military (SWAT) training, searched up to June 2024. Compared with controls, collar use was associated with less white matter alteration, better short-term neurocognitive results in some studies, and a larger internal jugular vein area, with no significant difference in concussion incidence.
paper.tldr: A 15-study review linked jugular vein compression collars to less white matter change and some better short-term cognitive results than controls, but found no difference in concussion incidence, and the evidence is low certainty.
paper.methods: A PRISMA-guided systematic review searched PubMed, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar for English-language observational and randomized studies published from 2000 to 2024, plus manual reference checks. Two reviewers extracted data independently, risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane RoB 2, and certainty of evidence was graded with GRADE.
paper.findings: White matter measures (MD, AD, RD, FA) were less favourable in control groups than collar groups in several studies. Internal jugular vein cross-sectional area increased from 0.10 to 0.57 cm2 with the collar in one study. Head impact exposure did not differ between groups in most studies, and concussion incidence did not differ (one study, very low certainty). Certainty for the other outcomes was low to moderate.
paper.limitations: Most participants were adolescents, and most included studies did not control for head impacts during off-seasons. Certainty was low to very low for most outcomes, several studies were funded by or involved the developer of the collar, and the synthesis is narrative with no pooled effect estimate.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not treat these collars as a proven concussion-prevention tool, because the review found no difference in concussion incidence and the imaging and cognitive findings are preliminary. Any use should be weighed against the evidence gaps and the device-related conflicts of interest the review reports.
paper.athleteDev: Performance application is limited: the review covers brain imaging and concussion-related outcomes rather than athletic performance, so it does not show that collars improve performance.
paper.rtp: The review does not evaluate return to sport or concussion recovery, so it cannot be used to guide return-to-play decisions or clearance after a concussion.
